summary: Describes provisioning models, auto-discovery, and signaling for provider-provisioned Layer 2 VPNs, where discovery distributes the configuration and signaling then sets up the mesh of pseudowires.

plainLanguage.summary: A carrier makes private links between customers' sites. This explains how it configures sites, finds out which belong together, and builds the connections automatically.

questions: what is bgp auto-discovery for vpls
subtitle: How layer 2 VPN endpoints are named, discovered with BGP and connected with LDP or L2TPv3 pseudowires.

tldr.problem: Provider-provisioned layer 2 VPNs come in several kinds, each configured differently, yet the signaling protocols that build their pseudowires need one general way to name the endpoints.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines provisioning models and the structure of the endpoint identifiers each needs (an Attachment Group Identifier plus source and target Attachment Individual Identifiers), shows how BGP carries them in auto-discovery, and how LDP and L2TPv3 encode them.
tldr.outcome: A discovery step finds which endpoints belong together and signaling then sets up the pseudowire mesh automatically, including across autonomous systems.

today: RFC 6074 is a Proposed Standard and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Endpoint Identifiers and Forwarders
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) is a relationship between a pair of Forwarders. In simple Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) a Forwarder binds one PW to one Attachment Circuit. In Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) it binds a set of PWs to a set of Attachment Circuits and consults a MAC address table. Forwarders may also bind PWs to PWs, which is called splicing.

To set up a PW, the signaling protocol must let one Forwarder identify the other with an Attachment Identifier (AI). The Generalized ID FEC element from RFC 4447 carries a Source AI and a Target AI, built from a shared Attachment Group Identifier (AGI) plus a Source or Target Attachment Individual Identifier (SAII, TAII). L2TPv3 uses the same idea with the AGI AVP, Local End ID AVP and Remote End ID AVP. The AGI can be thought of as a VPN identifier.

The pair <PE router, AI> must be globally unique. To the signaling procedures the TAI is just an arbitrary string of bytes, a cookie; how a PE maps it to one of its circuits is a local matter. Two endpoints may start signaling the same PW at once, and LDP builds a PW from two unidirectional LSPs, so each PE needs to recognize when they belong together.
sections.plainLanguage: Every end of a connection has a name made of a group name plus its own name. The name is just a label the receiver looks up on its own list.

sections.title: Individual Point-to-Point Pseudowires
sections.content:
Two provisioning models are described. In double-sided provisioning, each Attachment Circuit gets a local name, a remote PE address and a remote name. The local name is signaled as the SAII, the remote name as the TAII, and the AGI is null. For two circuits to connect, each one's local name must be the other's remote name.

In single-sided provisioning with discovery, each circuit has a local name made of a VPN-ID (the AGI) and a unique AII, and only one side needs the remote name. No remote PE address is needed. Each PE advertises its local pairs during auto-discovery and matches them against its remote pairs. The benefit is that a circuit can move to another PE without reconfiguring the far end; the cost is that every circuit name is advertised individually, with no aggregation.

On receiving an LDP Label Mapping or L2TP ICRQ message, a PE checks the circuit named by the TAI. If it is already bound to a PW with a different PE, or to a different remote circuit, it replies with a Label Release or a CDN message and a status code saying so. These errors could result from misconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: Either both ends write down each other's names, or both just join the same club and one end says who it wants to talk to. If a line is already taken by someone else, the answer is a polite no.

sections.title: VPLS and BGP Auto-Discovery
sections.content:
In VPLS each Forwarder is a Virtual Switching Instance (VSI), and one PW is needed between each pair of VSIs in the same VPLS. Every VPLS has a globally unique VPLS-id, and every VSI has a VSI-ID, which can be the VPLS-id combined with a PE IP address.

For BGP-based auto-discovery, each PE advertises an NLRI of the form RD:PE_addr for each VSI, with itself as BGP next hop, an Extended Community carrying the VPLS-id (which MUST be transitive) and one or more Route Targets (RTs). A PE imports NLRIs whose RT matches one of its VSIs and learns the other PEs from the next hop. If any required element is missing, the update should be ignored. Giving a VSI several RTs allows more complex topologies such as hierarchical VPLS.

For signaling, the VPLS-id goes in the AGI, the PE address in the TAII, and the SAII MUST be set to the sending PE's address so the reverse half can be signaled. Only one PW can be set up per pair of VSIs this way. A PW can also end at a VSI on one side and a plain Attachment Circuit on the other, in which case each PW needs an SAII unique relative to the VSI-ID.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch shouts which club it is in and where it lives. Switches in the same club hear each other and call each one up.

sections.title: Colored Pools for Pseudowire Meshes
sections.content:
The Colored Pools model delivers VPWS automatically. Each PE has pools of Attachment Circuits, and each pool has a "color" (a kind of VPN-id) and a relative pool identifier that is unique within the color. A PW is created between every pair of pools of the same color, bound to one circuit from each pool, giving a full mesh of CE-to-CE circuits. A circuit may optionally be configured with a remote pool identifier so the same pairs are always bound.

BGP auto-discovery works as for VPLS, except that the NLRI is the RD plus a 4-byte pool identifier and the Extended Community carries a VPWS identifier. In signaling, the VPWS identifier is the AGI, the local pool identifier the SAII and the remote pool identifier the TAII. If a PW already links a circuit in the target pool to the same remote circuit, the PE refuses with the status "Attachment Circuit already bound to remote Attachment Circuit", so there is only one PW per pair of pools.

For a partial mesh, pools get import and export RTs, and the export RTs replace the color in the BGP updates. A pool with import RT X connects to every pool that exports X. In a hub-and-spoke example the hub exports RT_hub and imports RT_spoke, and the spokes do the reverse, so spokes never connect to each other.
sections.plainLanguage: Every group of wires has a color, and wires with the same color get joined. To build a hub with spokes, the hub and spokes use matching passwords so only hub and spoke pair up.

sections.title: Distributed VPLS and Splicing
sections.content:
In Distributed VPLS, the PE is split into a User-facing PE (U-PE), which holds the VSI, and a Network-facing PE (N-PE). Each U-PE keeps PWs to the other U-PEs but has one signaling connection, to its N-PE. Every U-PE to U-PE PW is three PWs spliced together: U-PE to N-PE, N-PE to N-PE and N-PE to U-PE. This does not reduce the number of PWs per U-PE, but it reduces the number of control connections.

Each U-PE is given a list of pairs telling it how many PWs to open to which address, and each N-PE gets a local list, a local numbering of its U-PEs and a remote list. The U-PE signals with the VPN-id as AGI, the PW number as SAII and a null TAII. The N-PE signals to a U-PE with a null SAII and the PW number as TAII. N-PE to N-PE PWs use the remote N-PE's IP address as TAII and are told apart by the SAII. It does not matter which U-PW is spliced to which N-PW as long as the counts match. Only N-PEs take part in BGP auto-discovery, and a normal non-distributed PE can interoperate by advertising one local U-PE per VPLS.

Splicing in an MPLS data plane is a label replace operation on the PW label, and the data path passes through the splicing nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each small office calling every other office, each one calls only its regional hub, and the hubs patch the calls together.

sections.title: Inter-AS Operation
sections.content:
The same mechanisms can span autonomous systems, following the options in RFC 4364. The first option uses multihop EBGP between PEs in different ASes, with labeled IPv4 /32 (or IPv6 /128) routes to the PEs distributed by the ASBRs. PEs then discover each other directly and open LDP sessions across the AS boundary.

The second option avoids many cross-border sessions. PEs send L2VPN NLRI by IBGP to an ASBR, ASBRs pass it by EBGP, and the PW is built in segments, with each ASBR splicing them as described in RFC 6073. This gives a full mesh of PWs without a full mesh of control connections, and the splicing points sit at the ASBRs. A third option reuses Distributed VPLS, treating PEs as U-PEs and border routers as N-PEs, so only the two border routers hold the inter-provider control connection.

All of these need providers to coordinate RTs and RDs, as in Layer 3 VPNs. For a VPLS or VPWS spanning providers, one provider must allocate the identifier and tell the others to use the same value.
sections.plainLanguage: When two phone companies connect, they can have every office call across, or just let one border desk connect the lines. Either way, they must agree on the club names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines identifiers and how they map into protocol fields, and states that this mapping does not create additional security issues. Security for the signaling protocols is covered by their own specifications (RFC 5036, RFC 4447, RFC 3931 and RFC 4667), and for BGP-based auto-discovery, including inter-AS issues, by RFC 4364.

L2VPNs using BGP auto-discovery may automate security setup as well. Specifying that is outside the scope of this document but is recommended as future work.
sections.plainLanguage: This document only decides what to call things, so it adds no new risks. The safety rules live in the documents for the tools it uses.

sections.title: IANA Assignments and BGP-AD Coexistence
sections.content:
IANA assigned the same AFI and SAFI as used by RFC 4761: AFI 25 (L2VPN) and SAFI 65. They are used for both VPLS and VPWS auto-discovery. Type 1 was assigned in both the AGI Type and AII Type registries for the formats defined here. Two LDP status codes and two L2TP CDN result codes were assigned for the "bound to different PE" and "bound to different remote Attachment Circuit" errors. Two Extended Community values were assigned for the Layer 2 VPN Identifier.

BGP-AD and VPLS-BGP (RFC 4761) use the same AFI/SAFI, so NLRI length is used to tell them apart. The BGP-AD NLRI is 12 bytes (an 8-byte RD and a 4-byte VSI-ID), while VPLS-BGP uses 17 bytes. BGP-AD implementations must ignore NLRI longer than 12 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers for these labels were registered in the official list, and the length of a message tells two similar systems apart.
